body:
Junagadh and the Uparkot Fort

Uparkot Fort is the historic fortified complex at Junagadh, near the Girnar hills. The site has a history extending well before the Chudasama period. It passed through different phases of occupation, repair and alteration.

The Chudasamas are associated with the fort's medieval history, but it would be incorrect to credit them with creating the entire ancient fortified site from the beginning. The proper distinction is between the earlier existence of Uparkot and its use and development under later regional rulers.

Fortifications protected a political centre by creating barriers against attack and by providing a defended place for people and supplies. Their usefulness also depended on access to water, particularly during a prolonged siege.

Navghan Kuvo: a water source for a fortified settlement

Navghan Kuvo is a notable historic well inside Uparkot. It is partly cut into rock, and its staircase descends in a spiral around the well shaft. The descent to the water level is approximately 52 m.

Its design provided access to water within the fortified enclosure. This was important because attackers could cut off ordinary routes to external water sources during a siege. A protected well helped the inhabitants of the fort survive such conditions for longer.

Navghan Kuvo is commonly dated to approximately 1026 CE, although official tourism descriptions also acknowledge accounts suggesting an older origin. Its precise construction date should therefore not be presented as certain. Its association with the Chudasama period is more useful for the present topic than an unqualified claim that a particular ruler built every part of it.

Adi Kadi Vav: a different water structure

Adi Kadi Vav is another distinctive historic water structure inside Uparkot. It is a 15th-century rock-cut stepwell with a long stairway carved through hard rock. Gujarat Tourism describes a descent of approximately 120 steps towards the well.

Navghan Kuvo and Adi Kadi Vav are separate structures. Both demonstrate the importance of water within a fortified settlement, but they differ in their stairway arrangements and commonly assigned dates.

Religious centres, trade and local society

Saurashtra contained settlements supported by agriculture, pastoral activity, local exchange and pilgrimage. A ruler's ability to maintain authority depended not only on fortifications but also on relations with the surrounding population and access to important routes and resources.

Somnath at Prabhas Patan was an important pilgrimage and temple centre in Saurashtra. Pilgrimage sites could attract traders, artisans, workers and visitors. Temples could receive donations and support local economic activity. The political importance of the route to Somnath helps explain why conflicts involving rulers of mainland Gujarat and Sorath were remembered in regional histories.

Junagadh and the nearby Girnar hills also formed an important religious and cultural landscape. The area was associated with different religious communities and institutions over time. These associations should not be interpreted as the exclusive creation of a single dynasty.

Court patronage in the later Chudasama period

By the 15th century, the Chudasama court at Junagadh participated in established traditions of royal cultural patronage. A Sanskrit composition praising Ra Mandalika reflects the importance attached to royal status, learning and courtly representation.

Such patronage shows that the Chudasamas were not merely military chiefs. Their court also used the cultural forms associated with recognised regional kingship. Nevertheless, a poem composed in praise of a ruler should not be treated as proof that every victory or achievement described in it occurred exactly as written.

Prelims focus

  • Uparkot Fort is located at Junagadh, near Girnar.
  • Uparkot existed before the Chudasama period and was used by successive rulers.
  • Navghan Kuvo: historic Uparkot well with a spiral descent of approximately 52 m.
  • Adi Kadi Vav: separate rock-cut stepwell at Uparkot, generally dated to the 15th century.
  • Somnath at Prabhas Patan was a major pilgrimage and temple centre in Saurashtra.
  • Trap: Navghan Kuvo and Adi Kadi Vav are not 2 names for the same structure.

[Sources: Gujarat Tourism, Uparkot Fort, About the Location and Brief History; Gujarat Tourism, Adi-Kadi Vav, About the Location; Gujarat Tourism, Navghan Kuwo, About the Location; Government of Gujarat, Junagadh District Administration, Navghan Kuvo; NCERT, Class 7, Our Pasts–II, 2020–21 edition, Chapter 6, Towns, Traders and Craftspersons, printed pp. 75–78; Samira Sheikh, State and Society in Gujarat, c. 1200–1500: The Making of a Region, University of Oxford, 2003, discussion of the Chudasama court, pp. 107–115; online sources consulted 19 November 2026.]

title: Uparkot, Water Resources and Cultural Life in Chudasama Saurashtra

body:
Why the Chavda and Chudasama histories intersect

The Chavdas and Chudasamas were different ruling families, but their histories connect through the rise of the Chaulukyas of Patan. The Chaulukyas succeeded the Chavdas in north Gujarat and later tried to extend their influence into Saurashtra, where the Chudasamas held regional power.

This produces 2 different political relationships. The first is succession: the Chaulukyas replaced the Chavdas at Patan. The second is competition: the Chaulukyas fought the Chudasamas over authority in Saurashtra.

Succession at Patan: Chavdas followed by Chaulukyas.
Political competition in Sorath: Chaulukyas against Chudasamas.

Three important stages of conflict

The 10th century: Mulraja I and Graharipu

Mulraja I established Chaulukya rule at Patan. Accounts of his campaign against Graharipu of Vanthali show the political importance of Saurashtra to rulers based in north Gujarat.

Traditional narratives explain the campaign partly through Graharipu's alleged mistreatment of pilgrims travelling to Somnath. This should be understood as a claim in the accounts of the conflict, rather than a completely verified explanation of its causes.

The basic political result reported in the Chaulukya tradition is a victory for Mulraja. It illustrates an attempt to bring a neighbouring regional ruler under greater outside influence.

The 12th century: Siddharaja Jayasimha and Khengar

Siddharaja Jayasimha was a powerful Chaulukya ruler of Patan. He is associated with a campaign against the Chudasama ruler Ra Khengar in Sorath.

Accounts of the conflict describe the defeat of Khengar and the extension of Chaulukya authority into the region. This demonstrates that the Chudasamas did not exercise unchallenged control over Saurashtra throughout their history.

The relationship is especially important for identifying dynasties correctly: Siddharaja was a Chaulukya ruler, while Khengar belonged to the Chudasama tradition.

The 15th century: Mandalika III and Mahmud Begada

The final major political transition occurred when Mahmud Begada, the Gujarat Sultan, defeated the Chudasama ruler of Junagadh in 1472 CE.

Unlike the earlier contests with the Chaulukyas, this conquest brought the ruling family's position as an independent regional power to an end. The Gujarat Sultanate moved towards more direct control in the region, while members of the former ruling family continued in a reduced position as local landholders.

Do not confuse the rulers named Mahmud

Two different rulers named Mahmud appear in medieval Gujarat history:

  • Mahmud of Ghazni: A ruler based outside Gujarat, known for raids into the Indian subcontinent, including the attack on Somnath in the early 11th century.
  • Mahmud Begada: A ruler of the Gujarat Sultanate associated with the conquest of Chudasama-held Junagadh in 1472 CE.

Their activities were separated by several centuries. The first is connected with the Ghaznavid raids; the second with the expansion of the Gujarat Sultanate.

How the regional political landscape changed

The long sequence begins with the Chavda establishment of Patan, continues with Chaulukya rule over a larger part of Gujarat, and includes the continuing efforts of the Chudasamas to maintain authority in Sorath. By the 15th century, the Gujarat Sultanate had become the dominant power confronting the Chudasama rulers of Junagadh.

These changes show that the political history of medieval Gujarat cannot be represented by a single, uninterrupted line of kings. Different regional rulers often existed at the same time, and control over particular territories could change repeatedly.

Prelims focus

  • Vanraj Chavda: foundation of Anhilwad Patan, traditionally in the mid-8th century.
  • Mulraja I: establishment of Chaulukya rule at Patan in the 10th century.
  • Graharipu: Chudasama ruler associated with conflict against Mulraja I.
  • Ra Khengar: Chudasama ruler associated with conflict against Siddharaja Jayasimha.
  • Ra Mandalika III: late Chudasama ruler of Junagadh.
  • 1472 CE: defeat of the Chudasama ruler by Gujarat Sultan Mahmud Begada.
  • Trap: Mahmud of Ghazni's Somnath raid and Mahmud Begada's conquest of Junagadh were separate events involving different rulers.

[Sources: Gazetteer of the Bombay Presidency, Vol. I, Part I, History of Gujarat, 1896, Part II, Chapter I, sections 38–44, and Chapter II, sections concerning Mulraja and Siddharaja Jayasimha; NCERT, Class 7, Our Pasts–II, 2020–21 edition, Chapter 2, New Kings and Kingdoms, printed p. 21; Samira Sheikh, Alliance, Genealogy and Political Power: The Cudasamas of Junagadh and the Sultans of Gujarat, The Medieval History Journal, Vol. 11, Issue 1, 2008, abstract; online sources consulted 19 November 2026.]

title: Political Conflicts and Dynastic Transitions in Medieval Gujarat
